name: MAX485 RS-485 Transceiver
summary: Half-duplex RS-485 driver and receiver, the usual way to get Modbus or a long serial run off a microcontroller.
notes: Half duplex: only one device may drive the bus at a time. DE high enables the driver, RE low enables the receiver. Tie them together and drive both from one GPIO.
Release DE as soon as the last stop bit is on the wire, not when the UART buffer empties. Letting DE linger is the single most common RS-485 bug, and it makes the bus look dead to every other node.
A is the non-inverting line and B is the inverting one. Swapping them gives you clean idle levels and nothing but framing errors, so it is worth labeling the terminal block.
Terminate with 120 ohm across A and B at each end of the cable, and only at the ends. Mid-run terminators load the bus.
Idle bias matters: with every driver off the bus floats and receivers see noise as start bits. Add a pull-up on A and a pull-down on B, around 680 ohm, somewhere on the segment.
The plain MAX485 is a full unit load, so 32 nodes. MAX487 and friends are quarter unit load and reach 128.
This chip is 5 V. Driving its DI from 3.3 V logic works, but RO comes back at 5 V and needs a divider into a 3.3 V micro. The MAX3485 avoids the whole problem.

pins.name: RE
pins.note: Usually tied to DE and driven by one GPIO.

pins.name: DE
pins.note: High to transmit. Drop it the moment the last stop bit is out.

pins.name: GND
pins.note: The bus needs a common ground reference as well as the differential pair.

pins.name: A
pins.note: Non-inverting. Idles high relative to B.

parts.why: Termination, and only at the two physical ends of the cable. Mid-run terminators load the bus.
Idle bias, so receivers see a defined state when no driver is enabled.
The other half of the idle bias pair.
Ties receive enable to drive enable so one GPIO controls direction.

circuit.note: Ground must be common across the bus as well as the differential pair. A and B alone work on the bench and fail over a long run.
